column4: The section joins an enraged fire, entry into it, and a warning; here Hell nearly bursts with rage and every arriving company is asked whether a warner came, making the whole alarm-to-fire sequence explicit.
The entrants admit that a warner did come but that they denied him; this supplies the exact failed response to the section's فَأَنذَرْتُكُمْ and its denier.

وَيَتَجَنَّبُهَا ٱلْأَشْقَى makes the most wretched avoid the reminder, whereas the section's most wary is made to avoid the fire; the shared distancing verb exposes the decisive difference in what each person puts aside.
The same ٱلْأَشْقَى then يَصْلَى ٱلنَّارَ ٱلْكُبْرَىٰ, directly pairing the section's wretched person with entering and enduring fire.
إِنَّهَا لَظَىٰ uses the section's flame-word as Hell's proper name, confirming that تَلَظَّىٰ evokes both blazing action and a named destination.
Lezā تَدْعُوا۟ مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ; the fire itself summons the one who turned his back, exactly joining the section's blazing fire to the posture of turning away from its alarm.
فَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱلنَّارَ commands people to place the section's protective taqwā between themselves and a fire fueled by people and stones.
قُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا turns the dictionary's protective layer into an active duty: build protection for oneself and one's household before the fire is reached.
ثُمَّ نُنَجِّى ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّقَوا۟ says that God rescues those who took protective heed, giving the saving action behind the section's passive وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا.
فَمَن زُحْزِحَ عَنِ ٱلنَّارِ stages salvation as being physically edged away from the fire, clarifying the section's causative “will be kept to the side.”

فَوَقَىٰهُمُ ٱللَّهُ شَرَّ ذَٰلِكَ ٱلْيَوْمِ makes God the agent who places protection around the givers described in 76:8-10, matching the section's move from self-protective taqwā to divine warding.
إِذِ ٱنۢبَعَثَ أَشْقَىٰهَا names Thamud's most wretched member immediately before the denial in 91:14, giving the section's ٱلْأَشْقَى a concrete predecessor.
فَكَذَّبُوهُ records Thamud's denial of its messenger beside 91:12's “most wretched,” so the section's wretched denier repeats the closing movement of the preceding surah.
Fire covers the condemned above and below, and God says ذَٰلِكَ يُخَوِّفُ ٱللَّهُ بِهِۦ عِبَادَهُۥ ... فَٱتَّقُونِ; the frightening fire is itself the alarm that calls forth a shield.
A building founded on taqwā is set against a crumbling bank that falls with its builder into Hellfire, making the protective layer and the twisted route to fire into rival structures.

Hoarded metal is heated in Hell and brands foreheads, جُنُوبُهُمْ, and backs; the bodily “side” that explains the shield-name in the section becomes exposed to fire when wealth is hoarded rather than given.

Dhul-Qarnayn heats iron until it becomes fire and pours molten copper over it to make the barrier requested in 18:94; this joins the section's fire-as-craft sense to an interposed defense against an approaching enemy.
A people report the threat of Gog and Magog and ask for a سَدًّا between the attackers and themselves, reproducing the section's enemy alarm and its required intervening layer.
He asks them to help with strength so that he can place a رَدْمًا between the two sides; this ayah supplies the cooperative precaution that the warning scene requires before 18:96's fire-forging.
The attackers can neither scale nor pierce the completed barrier, showing the defensive result of the alarm and the fire-crafted layer in 18:94-96.

An ant sees Solomon's host approaching, tells the ants to enter their dwellings, and they take shelter; it is a Quranic enactment of the section's model in which an alarm is completed only by precaution.
After literal clothing that covers nakedness, لِبَاسُ ٱلتَّقْوَىٰ is called best; this turns the section's naked signal and its taqwā-shield into two sides of one clothing image.
Garments تَقِيكُمُ ٱلْحَرَّ and armor تَقِيكُم بَأْسَكُمْ are literal intervening layers against heat and violence, concretizing both the fire-threat and the dictionary definition of و ق ي.
Those who remember God عَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ pray فَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ; bodily “sides,” the place of the section's shield-name, meet the explicit request for protection from fire.
The bearers of the Throne pray وَقِهِمْ عَذَابَ ٱلْجَحِيمِ for those who repent and follow God's way, directly asking God to perform the warding pictured in the section.
وَقِهِمُ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ broadens the same shield from Hell's fire to the evil acts and consequences that lead there, explaining what may be intercepted before the final danger.
وَوَقَىٰهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ عَذَابَ ٱلْجَحِيمِ states the section's two-stage protection directly: their Lord, rather than they themselves, wards the blaze away.
The saved speakers say God favored them and وَوَقَىٰنَا عَذَابَ ٱلسَّمُومِ, presenting rescue from scorching punishment as a received shield.
After saying the blessed will taste no further death, وَوَقَىٰهُمْ عَذَابَ ٱلْجَحِيمِ names divine warding as the reason the fire never becomes their abiding place.
God delivers ٱلَّذِينَ ٱتَّقَوا۟ so that evil does not touch them; this makes their prior taqwā and God's subsequent rescue the two actions joined in the section.
The unbelievers cannot يَكُفُّونَ the fire from their faces or backs and receive no help, a direct reversal of the effective shield and divine distancing promised to the wary.
The guilty see the fire, know they are about to fall into it, and find no مَصْرِفًا away from it; the missing route of diversion sharpens what وَسَيُجَنَّبُهَا grants.
فَوَقَىٰهُ ٱللَّهُ سَيِّـَٔاتِ مَا مَكَرُوا shows God actively warding the believing man from a hostile plot, while 40:46 supplies the fire that engulfs Pharaoh's people instead.
Pharaoh's people are exposed to the fire morning and evening and then ordered into the severest punishment; it completes 40:45's contrast between one person warded and his attackers enclosed by fire.
The protected people of 76:11 first give food despite loving it, so their warding is tied to the same giving posture that precedes taqwā in the section.
They say they feed only for وَجْهِ ٱللَّهِ and seek no return, supplying the face-of-God motive that links the section's giver to the protection in 76:11.
Their giving is accompanied by fear of a grim day; this ayah supplies the feared object against which God's warding in 76:11 answers.
The messenger is defined as نَذِيرٌ لَّكُم بَيْنَ يَدَىْ عَذَابٍ شَدِيدٍ, a warning voice positioned immediately in front of severe punishment like the section's solitary alarm before the fire.
إِنَّا أَنذَرْنَاكُمْ عَذَابًا قَرِيبًا warns of a near punishment on the day each person sees what his hands sent ahead, making the alarm an occasion for action before arrival.
فَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ شَقُوا۟ فَفِى ٱلنَّارِ directly places those marked by شقوة in the fire, confirming the section's lexical joining of wretchedness and burning.
The wretched remain there as long as the heavens and earth endure, elaborating the section's gloss of صلي as entering the fire and staying with it.
Fire scorches the condemned faces while they grimace within it; 23:105-106 then identify denial and their own شِقْوَتُنَا, making this the bodily fire-side of that sequence.
They are asked whether God's signs were recited and they used to deny them, supplying the failed reception of warning that leads to the fire in 23:104 and wretchedness in 23:106.
The people in the fire confess غَلَبَتْ عَلَيْنَا شِقْوَتُنَا and that they went astray, explicitly joining the section's wretchedness, crooked course, and fiery result.
Hell's people are neither finished by death nor granted any lightening of punishment, fully staging the section's sense of entering the fire and remaining under its severity.
While crying to be released, they are reminded that a lifetime for recollection and a نَذِير came to them; their continued confinement is traced to an alarm not acted upon.
At Hell's opened gates its keepers ask the arriving companies whether messengers came reciting signs and warning them; their admission reproduces the section's warning-before-entry sequence.
They are told to enter Hell's gates and remain there, contributing the actual admission and permanence after the warning inquiry of 39:71.
The condemned are told, “This is the fire you used to deny,” placing denial and the now-visible warned object in one confrontation.
ٱصْلَوْهَا فَٱصْبِرُوٓا۟ أَوْ لَا تَصْبِرُوا۟ makes entering the fire and enduring it explicit, closely matching the section's gloss of ص ل ي as suffering its heat and severity.
Whenever the defiantly disobedient try to leave the fire they are returned and told to taste what they denied, joining denial, entry, and inescapable residence.
The messenger says he warns only by revelation, but the deaf do not hear the call إِذَا مَا يُنذَرُونَ; it defines failed warning as a failure to receive and act on the signal.
فَفِرُّوٓا۟ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ إِنِّى لَكُم مِّنْهُ نَذِيرٌ مُّبِينٌ gives the warning its proper completion: hearing the alarm produces immediate movement toward safety.
Saqar is declared one of the greatest things, establishing the immense fire whose function the next ayah identifies as warning humankind.
نَذِيرًا لِّلْبَشَرِ makes the fire described in the surrounding passage itself a warning, collapsing the section's alarm and its fiery object into one sign.
The question “Have you considered the fire you kindle?” directs attention to fire itself, preparing its surprising function as a reminder in 56:73.
God asks whether people created its tree or He did, shifting kindled fire from a human tool to a divinely supplied sign before 56:73 names its purpose.
“We made it a reminder and a provision for travelers” makes ordinary fire both alarm and benefit, a revealing counterpart to the section's warned blaze.
When the blaze sees the condemned from far away they hear its rage and roaring; this Quranic fire is not only hot but angry, exactly developing the section's anger sense of blazing.
كُلَّمَا خَبَتْ زِدْنَاهُمْ سَعِيرًا says that whenever Hell's fire subsides it is increased in blaze, giving the section's quick, restless flame an image of continually renewed combustion.
Those cast into Hell hear it inhaling while it boils, supplying the moving and sounding flame just before 67:8 calls it nearly split by rage and asks about warning.
The condemned say that had they listened or reasoned they would not be companions of the blaze, stating precisely the precautionary step omitted after the warning of 67:8-9.
Lezā calls the one who gathered and hoarded, tying the named flame to the withholding of wealth that stands opposite the section's protected giver.
Those who hoard gold and silver are told to expect painful punishment; this is the explicit alarm before 9:35 heats their hoard in Hell and brands their sides.
God teaches the manufacture of armor لِتُحْصِنَكُم مِّنۢ بَأْسِكُمْ, turning craft into an intervening protection from hostile force just as the section's shield stands beside a warned person.
The smoke offers لَا ظَلِيلٍ وَلَا يُغْنِى مِنَ ٱللَّهَبِ: a seeming cover that neither shades nor protects from flame, exposing a false shield at the very edge of fire.
A wall is placed between believers and hypocrites, with mercy inside and punishment outside; it is a literal intervening layer that sorts who is sheltered from the threatened side.
The hypocrites find no ransom and their refuge is the fire, completing 57:13's wall scene by identifying the punishment outside it.
سَيَذَّكَّرُ مَن يَخْشَىٰ says the one who fears will take the reminder, supplying the successful hearing-and-precaution response opposite 87:11's avoidance.
وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱلنَّارَ ٱلَّتِىٓ أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكَافِرِينَ is a second direct imperative to put protective heed between oneself and a prepared fire.
The prayer وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ turns the shield root into a direct request that God ward off fire.
Believers ask وَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ after confessing faith, another explicit appeal for the divine side of the section's protection.
“This is the Hell you were promised” identifies the warned object immediately before 36:64 orders the deniers to enter it.
ٱصْلَوْهَا ٱلْيَوْمَ بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ orders entry into Hell because of disbelief, joining the section's ص ل ي action to rejection of the warning.
سَيَصْلَىٰ نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ combines the section's entry verb with a fire characterized by flame, bringing ص ل ي and its “pure flame” explanation into one wording.
The one inside the greatest fire neither dies nor lives, clarifying the continuing condition entailed by 87:12's يَصْلَى.
Who comes to God as a criminal has Hell, where he neither dies nor lives; this repeats the enduring-fire condition that the section attaches to entry.
The condemned want to emerge from the fire but cannot and have lasting punishment, making the absence of any effective escape the reverse of being kept away beforehand.
Whenever they try to leave the fire from anguish they are returned to it, dramatizing the section's gloss that the one made to enter remains attached to the fire.
The disowned followers see their deeds as regrets and are not coming out of the fire, giving permanent consequence to a failure that no later precaution can undo.
The criminals remain in Hell's punishment, a direct statement of the lasting residence contained in the section's ص ل ي gloss.
The punishment is not lightened and they despair within it, adding unrelieved severity to 43:74's permanence.
Hell is made visible to whoever sees, beginning a judgment scene that sorts the one who preferred the nearer life from the one who feared and restrained himself.
The transgressor prefers ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا, giving the choice that makes Hell his shelter in 79:39 and reversing the section's prior precaution.
فَإِنَّ ٱلْجَحِيمَ هِىَ ٱلْمَأْوَىٰ makes fire the transgressor's enclosing refuge, a grim inversion of the protective shelter sought by taqwā.
The other person fears standing before his Lord and restrains the self from desire, supplying the inward precaution that leads away from 79:39's fire.
فَإِنَّ ٱلْجَنَّةَ هِىَ ٱلْمَأْوَىٰ gives the fearful person a true refuge opposite the fire-refuge of 79:39.
Those who submit تَحَرَّوْا۟ رَشَدًا, deliberately seeking right direction; 72:15 then makes the deviating group fuel for Hell, closely joining straight course and fiery end.
The قَاسِطُونَ, those who deviate, become firewood for Hell, a concrete parallel to the section's crooked course arriving at the craftsman's fire.
“Guide them to the path of Hellfire” turns direction itself into an arrival at fire, illuminating the section's paradox of being facilitated along the difficult, twisted route.
The person who gathers and repeatedly counts wealth supplies the withholding posture whose destination is God's kindled fire in 104:6.
نَارُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْمُوقَدَةُ gives the hoarder's destination as God's kindled fire, joining withheld wealth to active ignition.
The fire is مُؤْصَدَةٌ عَلَيْهِم, closed over them, making the enclosing layer itself punishment rather than protection.
A fire whose surrounding pavilion encloses the wrongdoers turns a shelter-like boundary into the fire's own wall, the inverse of the section's saving barrier.
وَإِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمُحِيطَةٌ بِٱلْكَافِرِينَ makes Hell the encompassing layer, reversing taqwā's enclosure against what is feared.
Punishment covers them from above and from beneath their feet, supplying the spatial completion of Hell's encirclement in 29:54.
Hell is both a bed beneath and coverings above the wrongdoers; the layers that would ordinarily shelter instead become fire.
ثُمَّ ٱلْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ orders the denier into the blaze, using the same entry-and-burning root as the section.
The person sent into the blaze did not believe in God, supplying refusal as one cause of 69:31's fiery entry.
He also did not urge feeding the poor, placing refusal to give beside entry into the blaze and thereby reversing the section's protected giver.
Who follows God's guidance neither goes astray nor يَشْقَىٰ, making freedom from wretchedness the result of taking the directed path rather than turning from it.
Who turns away from God's reminder receives a constrained life, tying the section's turning away to lived hardship before the final fire.
God answers that signs came but were forgotten, supplying the rejected signal that explains the hardship of 20:124 and the loss of guidance in 20:123.
The trumpet's day is called يَوْمٌ عَسِيرٌ, bringing the section's hardship word into the same surah that presents Saqar as a warning.
That day is “not easy” for the unbelievers, explicitly opposing عَسِير to ease and clarifying who experiences the section's destination of hardship.

A kindled fire first illuminates its surroundings, then God removes their light; this directly exposes the section's dictionary link between fire and trembling light while showing that illumination need not become guidance.
Punishment comes suddenly, stuns them, and they can neither repel it nor gain respite; it is the hostile surprise for which the section's advance alarm and shield are needed.
People are told to follow the best revelation before punishment comes suddenly while they are unaware, stating the practical precaution that must follow warning.
Opposite 11:106's ٱلَّذِينَ شَقُوا۟, ٱلَّذِينَ سُعِدُوا۟ are in the Garden; this is the Quranic realization of the section's dictionary claim that wretchedness is the contrary of happiness.
A condemned person tries to يَتَّقِى بِوَجْهِهِۦ the evil punishment with his face; this grotesque last-minute “shield” contrasts with taqwā established before danger.
The wrongdoers have no وَاقٍ from God, stating the absence of precisely the protecting agent promised to the section's wary person.
The lamp's oil nearly glows وَلَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نَارٌ; light stands at the boundary of fire without being touched by it, a luminous counter-image to the section's fire named from flickering light.

When the people turn away, the messenger says he has warned them of a thunderbolt like those of ʿAd and Thamud; the threatened object differs from fire, but the immediate turn-away after a specific alarm matches the section's failed response.
The one walking fallen on his face is contrasted with one walking upright on a straight path, supplying the bodily geometry behind the section's twisted route and its need for straightening.

وَمَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِۦ makes greed an inward danger from which one must be shielded; because the ayah praises giving preference to others, it identifies a barrier that precedes the section's fire-shield.

After commanding taqwā, listening, obedience, and giving, the ayah says whoever is shielded from the self's greed succeeds; it joins the section's giving and protective roots inside one moral sequence.
مَآ أَنزَلْنَا عَلَيْكَ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ لِتَشْقَىٰ denies that revelation was sent to make the messenger wretched; the warning is therefore the rescue from شقاء, not its cause.
The revelation is instead a reminder for one who fears, completing 20:2's contrast and matching the section's idea that fear should produce receptive precaution.
Adam's children are warned that Satan stripped their parents' clothing; beside 7:26's garment of taqwā, the lost covering becomes a caution about allowing the protective layer to be removed.
David is told to make full coats of mail and measure their links, another craft scene in which carefully shaped material becomes protection from violence.

Material heated in fire for ornaments or tools throws off scum; although no punishment is involved, this is a Quranic instance of fire used by a craftsperson to work material, illuminating the section's secondary ص ل ي sense.
فَمَآ أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ ironically asks how they can endure the fire after trading guidance away, closely touching the section's sense of suffering and remaining under its heat.

Moses sees a fire at a distance and hopes to bring a brand or find guidance there; as a plausible counter-image, distant fire functions as a visible signal toward guidance rather than the warned destination.

Moses tells his family he perceives a fire and may return with news or a burning brand for warmth; the specific link is the section's far-visible signal and moving flame, though here the fire promises aid rather than danger.

Moses notices fire from the side of the mount and seeks news or an ember; this may echo the section's remotely legible signal, but its narrative role is guidance and warmth, not threatened punishment.
God knows which faction is most deserving of burning in Hell; this supplies the ص ل ي action immediately before 19:71's approach and 19:72's rescue of those who took protective heed.
Every person is brought to or passes over Hell before 19:72 distinguishes those God rescues for their taqwā, making divine removal from danger the climax of an actual approach to it.
Lezā is described as stripping away the skin or scalp, giving the named pure flame of 70:15 a bodily action before it calls the one who turned away in 70:17.
Those who consume orphan wealth unjustly consume fire into their bellies and will burn in a blaze, joining wrongful acquisition, internalized fire, and the section's ص ل ي action.
One who commits the prohibited act in aggression and injustice is promised admission to fire, another direct use of the section's burning-entry root with the conduct that leads there.
The skins of those burned in fire are repeatedly replaced so that they continue to taste punishment, concretizing the section's gloss of enduring the fire's heat and severity.
One who opposes the messenger after guidance is clear and follows another way is turned toward that choice and burned in Hell, directly joining a deviating route to fiery arrival.
Those who disbelieve and do wrong are denied guidance to a way, setting up 4:169's sole remaining path to Hell and tying rejection to misdirection.
The only path left to the deniers is the path of Hell, where they remain, closely paralleling the section's twisted course that terminates in fire.
The prayer says that whoever God admits into the fire is disgraced and has no helpers, clarifying admission as the opposite of being warded and moved aside.
The wicked burn in Hell on the Day of Judgment, using the section's ص ل ي root for their actual entry into fire.
They are never absent from that fire, adding the permanence contained in the section's explanation of entering and staying.
Whether the condemned endure patiently or not, the fire remains their dwelling and no appeal restores favor; this makes endurance powerless once the alarm has been ignored.
Messengers recount God's signs, and whoever takes protective heed and reforms has no fear; the ayah supplies the successful response before 7:36 gives the denier's fiery result.
Those who deny the signs and act arrogantly toward them become abiding companions of the fire, completing 7:35's warning-and-taqwā alternative.
The people are told to take protective heed of what lies before and behind them so that they may receive mercy, framing taqwā as spatial precaution against approaching danger.
No sign comes from their Lord without their turning away from it, supplying the failed response to the precautionary alarm in 36:45.

Abraham asks God to keep him and his children apart from idol worship; the causative form of ج ن ب shows divine distancing as protection, although the object avoided is an antecedent of punishment rather than the fire itself.
Every nation receives a messenger commanding worship of God and avoidance of false powers; warning and deliberate اجتناب are joined as the path of precaution.
Their sides leave their beds as they call on God in fear and hope and spend from His provision; the bodily “side” named in the shield gloss meets fear, action, and giving in one posture.
God says He will burn the rejecting man in Saqar, a direct use of the section's fire-entry root within the passage that later calls Saqar a warning to humanity.
Those who deny the Hour have a blaze prepared for them, placing denial of the warning's horizon immediately before the enraged fire that sees them from afar in 25:12.
The revelation warns the central city and those around it of the gathering day, when one group is in the Garden and another in the blaze; warning and the two destinations are stated together.
At the gathering, the people allied with jinn are assigned the fire as their abode; 6:130 later asks whether messengers warned them of this very meeting.

The gathered communities are asked whether messengers recited the signs and warned them of their meeting that day, and they testify against themselves; it supplies the acknowledged alarm behind 6:128's fire.
The polytheists call toward the fire whereas God calls toward the Garden and forgiveness, exposing two rival summons and the destination reached by answering each.
The oppressive leaders are made leaders who call people to the fire, a human counter-call to the warning voice that seeks to move hearers away from it.
The believing man asks why he calls his people to salvation while they call him to the fire, stating the section's opposed directions as rival spoken appeals.
Satan is an enemy whose party-call aims to make people companions of the blaze, joining the hostile threat, a summons, and fiery destination.
Those who practiced taqwā are conducted to the Garden in groups, forming the protected counterpart to the groups driven to Hell after their warning in 39:71-72.
God's kindled fire rises over the hearts, adding an inward reach to the hoarder's fire before 104:8 closes it over them.
The fire is closed over them in extended columns, completing the enclosure announced in 104:8 with the structure that seals it.

Those outside the wall are told that they tempted themselves, waited, doubted, and were deceived until God's command came, explaining the failed precaution that placed them on 57:13's punishment side.
The person whose refuge becomes Hell first transgresses, contributing the initiating act before 79:38 names preference for the nearer life and 79:39 names the fire.
Garments of fire are cut for the disbelieving party and boiling liquid is poured over their heads, turning an ordinarily protective layer into the punishment itself.
The poured heat melts what is inside their bellies and their skins, specifying the fire's severity before 22:22 describes their failed attempts to leave it.
Those who exchange God's favor for disbelief lead their people to ruin, Hell, which they enter and burn in; misdirection by a leader ends in the section's ص ل ي action.
The wrongdoers, their counterparts, and what they worship are gathered together before 37:23 directs them to Hell's path, supplying the company being marched toward that destination.
The messenger is asked whether he can rescue someone already in the fire after the sentence has taken effect; the impossible rescue contrasts with God's promised warding before entry.
One person is cast into the fire while another arrives secure on Resurrection Day, setting fiery admission and protected arrival side by side.

The expelled people thought their fortresses would protect them, but judgment reached them from where they did not expect; the failed external barrier clarifies why the section locates effective protection in taqwā and God's warding.

Those who keep themselves away from false powers and turn to God receive good news; their self-directed اجتناب shows the same distancing motion that the wretched misdirect toward the reminder in 87:11.
Joseph's interpretation instructs sustained sowing and protected storage before the announced famine, a specific nonlexical parallel to warning becoming complete through practical precaution.
The seven hard years then consume what was stored except a protected remainder, showing why the advance measures ordered in 12:47 constitute an effective shield.
The community is told to take protective heed of a trial that will not strike only the wrongdoers, extending taqwā from personal fear to precaution against a danger that can overrun a whole group.
Each soul is commanded to inspect what it has sent ahead for tomorrow while repeating the call to taqwā, explicitly making foresight and preparation the response to future danger.
Humbled faces burn in an intensely hot fire, a compact repeated formulation of the section's entry verb together with the heat it must endure.
The one receiving the record behind the back cries for destruction and burns in a blaze, another contextualized occurrence of the section's ص ل ي action.
Those veiled from their Lord then burn in Hell, using the same root for entry while adding exclusion from divine presence as the condition preceding it.
